content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
An effective method used for image-text retrieval, i.e., AVSE, is proposed to solve the inaccurate similarity measurement caused by some inherent variations, e.g., information density, which utilizes the multi-view to alleviate such effect and enhance image representation for higher performance.

The key contributions:
1. A effective method, AVSE, achieves higher performance while achieving fast inference.
2. AEOM is proposed for the optimization of the multi-view concatenate features.
3. A dimension-wise regularizing for different views.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
1. The related works are well summarized.
2. The experimental results look great.
3. The method has a certain novelty.

Cons:
1. Rationality: As described and summarized by the authors in related works, in fact, (NAAF, GSMN, etc.) and (VSRN, VSE $\infty$, the proposed AVSE) belongs to the two groups of image-text retrieval methods, so it is unfair and unreasonable to compare their inference time. reasonable. At the same time, compared with Global-level matching methods, such as VSRN and VSE $\infty$, AVSE spends more inference time, which is not enough to reflect the advantage of AVSE retrieval efficiency, but it is emphasized many times in the text.
2. Fairness: AVSE uses the same pre-trained glove features as NAAF (I remember that NAAF also announced pre-trained models without glove.) for embedding initialization, which actually improves performance. However, in the baselines, SGRAF, IMRAM, SCAN, etc. are not initialized with Glove. I hope the author can provide a fair competition for the result of AVSE without using gloves.
3. In the ablation study, it can be found that when the number of views increases, the selection of the most suitable visual information should be more reasonable, and the performance should be better. However, when using AEOM, why is the performance not better as the number of views increases? If it can't be explained well, I have reason to think that it is not AEOM that solves the information difference between modalities, but multi-view complementation or enhancement (this is actually equivalent to increasing the dimension of visual features, such as 2x1024, which is also possible to obtain better performance), not the role of this particular module (AEOM). In other words, two VSE $\infty$ models initialized with Glove to train two independent views respectively, and then ensemble the similarity for retrieval, will there be better performance?
4. Training time: In AVSE, a larger matrix is actually used to connect multiple visual views and calculate the affinity matrix between views, which seems to be time-consuming. 
5. The hyper-parameter $\lambda$ in dimension-wise regularization is 0.0051 in the experiments, which seems to be a not very common empirical setting. Could the authors provide a reasonable explanation, preferably a parametric analysis of $\lambda$?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is well-written and easy to follow. However, this work lacks novelty.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper utilizes the concept of multiple views to achieve more reasonable visual feature embedding to achieve high performance of image-text retrieval, but I have some concerns (see Cons). If my concerns are addressed, I will consider increasing the score appropriately.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents an asymmetric visual embedding to learn visual semantic similarity based on the difference in information density
between the text and visual modalities and avoid costly computations. The proposed Asymmetric Visual Semantic Embedding (AVSE) considers the abundant image regions from multi-views to learn the image embedding in a concatenating way. The authors also design the asymmetric embedding optimal matching module to efficiently calculate the semantic similarity. The proposed approach looks to have promising results compared to the state-of-the-art methods on two benchmarks, MS-COCO and Flickr30K.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: Overall, the paper introduces asymmetric embedding (different dimensions between text and image) and several off-the-shelf algorithms and explains their motivations and problems, the idea of visual representation with multiple views sounds reasonable and the designed asymmetric embedding optimal matching may make sense too. In addition, the authors show the proposed model also improves the computational efficiency in the inference process compared to some state-of-the-art methods.

Weaknesses: Several items reduce the paper quality. 1) it's good to consider multiple views from an image, but I'd like to know why the paper only discussed the grouping by two, is there any experiment to show different numbers among different datasets? 2) For the text feature extraction, are all the compared methods using the same features? Is there any discussion about why the authors choose the GloVe vector? 3) why do the authors choose Faster R-CNN? Will it be better if adopt the most recent state-of-the-art/different methods? 4) what is the main reason for the inference speed improvement? The inference efficiency analysis subsection mentioned it's due to the proposed method belonging to the global-level matching method, but I'd like to know how the dynamically computing improves the inference time.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The overall quality level of the paper is good: it is clear to read in sections, but some parts that may not be clear such as the definition of $a$ and $b$ in Section 3.2. The index $j$ in equations (3), equations (4), and (5), etc. The proposed method considers the multiple views from an image and joins it with the existing hinge-based triple loss for optimization. The novelty of this paper may be limited since it looks like a combination of work with objection detection, text feature extraction, and the joint loss function. Moreover, two benchmarks may be okay, but it'll be better to show with more datasets.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper investigates a different way to cooperate with multiple views from an image and proposed an asymmetric visual semantic embedding (AVSE) for image-text retrieval. To exploit the information density difference between the two modalities, the proposed method design a similarity learning module by combining the existing triple loss to optimize the matching between text and visual blocks. The experimental results show promising results in two benchmarks.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an asymmetric visual-semantic embedding learning approach, motivated by the fact that an image might be described in multiple ways in language form. The approach encodes multiple views of an image, and performs matching against a single text embedding using a so-called Asymmetric Embedding Optimal Matching (AEOM) module.  Experiments are conducted on Flickr30K and MS-COCO datasets with comparison to prior visual-semantic embeddings and ablation studies.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
 * Good motivation and intuitive approach.

Weakness
 *  AEOM module seems overly complex and unnecessary. Dividing embedding dimension into blocks seems arbitrary. A simpler approach would be just taking the max matching score between the semantic embedding and the embedding of an image views. Ablation study shows that d2=512 performs the best, but what about d2=d1=1024 (no blocks)? It's also questionable to use mean pooling across views in the ablation of AEOM.
 * Experimental setup was a bit dated and hence not sufficiently convincing
    - Modern approaches usually pre-trains on much larger datasets (e.g. CLIP)
    - Transformer/BERT based text embeddings
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarify: OK but could be improved. For instance, "n" in Section 3.2 doesn't have any explanation (I believe it is the number of views as in Section 3.1)

Novelty: somewhat novel

Reproducibility: good
content.summary_of_the_review: While asymmetric visual-semantic embedding is well motivated, the key contribution of the paper -- AEOM seems not technically sound.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3881 by Reviewer pQQE

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a method for learning image-text embeddings for cross-modal retrieval. The key thesis is that there is an "information density" difference between images and text. That is to say, the same image can be described with different pieces of text depending on what the viewer tends to focus on in the description (i.e. the main object, something in the background, an activity, etc.). The authors argue that this information density issue makes it difficult to learn a single global embedding that accurately representings all the semantics of the image. 
The authors propose a method for addressing the information density difference. The method learns, what are called, "Asymmetric" visual semantic embeddings which essentially decompose an image's representation into sub-chunks and find the best alignment with the text representation - thus accounting for different focuses or views of the image.
The way this specifically works is by taking object proposal embeddings from the image and concatenating them. The authors then break the concatenated embedding into "blocks" and also break the text embedding into blocks (just chucks of the embedding). Then, the authors compute an affinity matrix between the image and text blocks using Sinkhorn algorithm. Once they have the correspondences, they essentially use those aligned "blocks" to compute the distance.
The authors experimentally validate their method on MSCOCO and Flickr30k datasets and show SOTA or competitive performance against a number of recent SOTA baseline methods for image to text and text to image retrieval.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strengths]
The idea that images can be described from different "perspectives" is a very interesting one. The authors propose a method to address this very real problem in a very elegant way. The idea is essentially to find the best "correspondences" between semantic text and image features. The way they do this is technically novel - by using a decomposition of the image and text embeddings and finding an alignment using optimal transport and then measuring distance.

One of my key concerns when reading the paper was the speed of the authors' technique. After all, the decomposition requires an alignment with the text embedding and if there are many possible alignments, one will need to compute this alignment repeatedly - i.e. resulting in additional computational overhead compared to methods where one can simply run a cosine distance matrix multiplication between image and text embeddings to do the retrieval. However, the authors extensively address this concern by show how their method adds little such overhead - for example, when there are 1000 candidates, the method adds only 0.3 seconds, which is a 1000x speedup compared to several other baselines.

Authors also provide a number of ablation experiments, testing various hyperparameters of their model and ablate their design choices. These ablations demonstrate the importance of their proposed contributions. Authors also provide qualitative results showing attention to what image regions their model selects for the different views.

Experimentally, the authors' method, when ensembled, outperforms most other ensembled benchmarks on the two benchmark datasets compared against. When not ensembled, the authors' method still performs competitively and outperforms or is highly competitive to non-ensembled baselines.

[Weaknesses]
I believe authors should cite Polysemous Visual Semantic Embeddings (Song et al) whose paper has a similar idea. For example, the idea in PVSE is that each image or text can have multiple meanings. To account for this, PVSE learns multiple embeddings for each image and for each text and then simply chooses the best aligned version. This could be seen as a variant of what the authors' method is doing. While the authors evaluate their method on COCO and Flickr30k, I am wondering how well the authors method would work on these more challenging image-text retrieval tasks that specifically target the scenario when the text or image has multiple meanings. For example, "Preserving Semantic Neighborhoods for Robust Cross-modal Retrieval" focuses on the task of retrieving images or text when the image or text is complementary or has different perspectives. To me, this evaluation scenario seems like a strong selling point of the authors' method. After all, if the image and text are very straightforward, authors' motivation might be weaker since their may be less perspectives from which to describe the image.

Authors choose Glove fed into a GRU as their text embedding. Why not use a more recent contextualized representation for the text embedding? Glove / GRU is quite old. A transformer-based representation might work better?

On the subject of text representation, while the authors decompose the image into multiple "perspectives" or (as they call it - views), what about the text? Surely there are some cases where the text could be interpreted multiple ways - particularly in the case of real-world captions (as described in the Robust Cross-modal Retrieval paper above). In that case, the text could be longer or more abstract and choosing a focus could be important. Why don't authors also break the text embedding into different "views"?

Is there a better way to do the groupings of features than "random"? What about ensuring the groups are semantically diverse? It seems the random groupings might cause objects associated with different perspectives to leak into the other perspective when they really shouldn't be included (i.e. if you are describing something from one perspective, objects from the other perspective could appear in that group unnaturally).

The motivation for section 3.3 is very unclear to me. The text is also hard to follow here. Can you explain what this dimension-wise regularization is doing intuitively and why it is needed?

While authors show good results for retrieval, what about the utility of these embeddings for other downstream tasks? Can they be used for those types of things, i.e. fed into a downstream model for zero-shot recognition, for example?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The contribution is of high quality. The method is of moderate technical novelty and the design of the technique is well-motivated.
As for clarity, the paper is, at times, hard to follow. I would advise the authors to reconsider the word "views" and perhaps describe this as describing the image from different semantic perspectives. "Views" could be confusing.
The method is described in detail and implementation details are provided. Thus the paper should be reproducible. The experiments, paper, and materials are of high quality sufficient for ICLR.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, the authors propose an interesting method for cross-modal retrieval. The key idea is that the same image can be described in different ways. The authors' method naturally addresses this problem, though does not address the fact that text could exhibit the same behavior. Critically, the authors' method performs very fast and adds little computational overhead. Technically, the method offers moderate novelty and is interesting. The authors soundly evaluate their method and demonstrate moderate gains. While some aspects of the evaluation could be improved, such as by evaluating on more "polysemous" data, the paper is solid and presents a good contribution to the field.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
